h1: Hydraulic, electric and CNC folding machines — 10 ga over 10 ft, 14 ga CNC over 12 ft
intro: A powered folding machine clamps and folds the sheet with hydraulic cylinders or electric drives, so a 10 ft bend in 10 ga takes a foot pedal instead of two people and a CNC folder runs a 99-bend program with its back gauge while the operator only turns and feeds the sheet. NovoTech sells three kinds in Canada, all on this page: HW hydraulic folding machines, 10 ga over 4 to 10 ft and 3/16″ over 80 – 100″, with a hydraulic clamping beam, a folding beam driven by cylinders and a segmented upper beam on the box models; EFM / EFMS electric folding machines, 16 to 20 ga over 80 – 120″, for the shop that wants power without hydraulics; and TFM / TFMS CNC electric folders, 14 ga over 122 and 145″, with a CNC back gauge to 48″ and ±0.004″ repeatability for production panels, cassettes and enclosures. Every model is in the table below with its length, capacity and weight, then each family with its full specification and photos. NovoTech's value-line machines are built in China to our specification, with parts and support from Mississauga, ON, Canada.

faq.q: When should I buy a folding machine instead of a press brake?
faq.a: When the work is long panels in thin and medium sheet — duct, enclosures, architectural cladding, flashing — up to 10 ga. A folder bends from one side with the sheet lying flat, so a long panel needs no support or second person, there are no punch and die to change, and painted sheet is not marked. A press brake is the better machine for short heavy parts, for thick plate, for many different bends in one part and for tight tolerances on small flanges.

Hydraulic for the heaviest work — 10 ga over 10 ft and 3/16″ over 8 ft — and the lowest price per foot of capacity. Electric for 16 – 20 ga sheet where the shop wants powered clamping and folding without a hydraulic unit, oil or a three-phase pump. CNC when the same panels are made every day: the back gauge positions each flange from the program, the angle is corrected for springback and radii are folded in small steps, so an unskilled operator makes the part right first time.

faq.q: What does a CNC folding machine add?
faq.a: A CNC folder (TFM, TFMS) positions the back gauge for every flange and folds to a programmed angle, one bend after the other from a program of up to 99 bends — the operator only turns and feeds the sheet. Programs are stored for repeat parts, the control corrects the angle for springback and folds radii in small steps. It pays for itself on production panels — cladding, cassettes, enclosures, duct — where a hand-set folder needs a skilled operator for every part. The TFMS has a segmented upper beam for boxes.

faq.q: How are the capacities rated, and what about stainless and aluminum?
faq.a: In gauge (or inches) of mild steel over the full bending length; the specification tables give the stainless rating separately — about two gauges lighter — and aluminum goes about two gauges heavier. Folding at less than full length lets the machine take somewhat heavier sheet.

faq.q: Can a folding machine fold painted or coated sheet without marking it?
faq.a: Yes — that is one of the reasons to fold instead of press-brake bending: the sheet is clamped and the beam swings around the clamp edge without sliding over a die. Protective film on the sheet keeps pre-painted and brushed stainless perfect.

faq.q: What voltage do these machines run on?
faq.a: Three-phase machines are supplied for 600 V as standard with a CSA-approved panel; 208 V, 240 V and 480 V 3-phase are available on request, and 240 V single-phase on models with a small enough motor. Manual machines have no electrics.
